items.title: Should you build or buy your mobile release management platform?
items.summary: Building internal mobile release tooling looks like a two-quarter project. It almost never is. Why the build vs. buy math almost always favors buying.

items.title: How to upload assets using the App Store Connect API
items.summary: A detailed guide showing how to automate the upload of screenshots and other media assets using the App Store Connect API.

items.title: How to build the perfect mobile release train
items.summary: Release trains are not a silver bullet to solve all your problems, but they can help you ship new versions of your app more predictably, reduce risk, get feedback from users faster, and improve collaboration and planning within your team.

items.title: Avoiding release anxiety, part II
items.summary: Regardless of the tools and processes you're using, you'll find that the best resource you can have to make a project anxiety-free are the people working with you. You can have the best testing practices, the best architectural concepts and the world's most finely-tuned CI, but if you're not aligned with your team, things will probably not go as intended.

items.title: Mobile app release process best practices: visibility, coordination, and scale
items.summary: For most mobile teams, release processes are set up early and rarely revisited. That is, until they start causing real pain. Missed deadlines, last-minute scrambles, and knowledge siloed in one engineer's head are all symptoms of a process that hasn't kept pace with the team as the org scales. The teams that ship consistently and confidently are the ones that treat their release process as infrastructure worth investing in.

items.title: Why you should shift left when testing your mobile app
items.summary: Shift left is about more than just testing your code and your user experience, it’s also part of a philosophy of bringing development, security, and operations (DevSecOps) to every single stage of development. Shift left is particularly impactful for mobile teams because mobile app updates have inherently slower release cycles. The App Store review process and slower adoption of updates across devices mean it takes longer to find and fix issues that are discovered later in the development cycle. This means issues have a bigger impact on users, and we know that mobile app users in general are less tolerant of buggy, crashy apps.

items.title: Why CI/CD won’t save your mobile team
items.summary: Surprising as it may seem, and while the scale and stakes might differ, it turns out a lot can be learned from aerospace about the role of automation and its impact on the humans involved: from its initial rise and specific applications, to the friction and risks its ever-growing importance created, to the kinds of solutions and measures put in place to ensure its safe and effective use.

items.title: How much time do mobile engineers really lose per release?
items.summary: Mobile engineers lose 5 hours per release to manual work. On highly-automated teams, 6-10 is common. Runway's 2025 data shows where the time goes and how to calculate the real cost.

items.title: Is there such a thing as releasing mobile updates too fast and too often?
items.summary: It's common for companies to release new versions of their apps very frequently to address bugs, add new features, and act on user feedback. While this sounds like a good approach in theory, can releasing your app too often be detrimental to your app's success?

items.title: The Runway 2024 year in review
items.summary: In 2024 we built more big features, a lot more enhancements, and a longer list of new automations & integrations than any year before. See all the highlights.

items.title: Build vs. buy for mobile release tooling: lessons from Monzo, Spotify, Tuist, and Etsy
items.summary: There's no clean threshold for when to build vs. buy mobile release tooling. In a live panel, senior engineers from Monzo, Spotify, Tuist, and Etsy explained why the real cost is ongoing maintenance and coordination — not the first build — and why AI accelerates that trap rather than removing it.

items.title: Introducing Flightpaths by Runway
items.summary: Flightpaths unlocks entirely new ways to set up, manage, and automate your end-to-end release cycles. Your team has complete control, with the ability to rearrange release steps, leverage multiple steps of the same type for different parts of your cycle, and define more complex dependency graphs between steps. Under the hood, it’s a complete re-architecture of Runway designed for flexibility at scale.

items.title: How to improve visibility and coordination across your mobile release process
items.summary: Most mobile teams accept poor release visibility as the cost of doing business. But the coordination tax compounds fast and the fix starts with infrastructure, not effort.

items.title: Mobile releases are broken for engineers. Why are we ok with this?
items.summary: There’s a reason almost every mobile engineer dreads their turn running releases. In fact, there are several reasons that they dread it. Releasing mobile apps is a broken process, barely held together by duct-taped checklists and hand-crafted scripts that bleed engineers of their time and companies of their money.

items.title: Mobile teams are second-class citizens, but not on purpose
items.summary: Mobile teams are still catching up with their web developer colleagues. Not in terms of skill or contributions to their orgs, but in their access to tooling and infrastructure that supports their feature work. How do we fix that?

items.title: 2025 State of Mobile Release Management Report
items.summary: For mobile-driven businesses, releases define the pace and reliability of your product. Our new report outlines the patterns that slow teams down, and the playbooks high performers rely on.

items.title: Rollbacks on mobile: yes, they’re possible, and this is why you need them
items.summary: The nature of mobile releases makes implementing a true rollback mechanism inherently impossible. But luckily, with a bit of effort, a very close approximation to rollbacks can be achieved. Here's how.

items.title: What should you do when something goes wrong with your mobile app, besides panic?
items.summary: No matter how well you prepare, how thoroughly you test, and how carefully you roll out, there will come a day (or several days) when your mobile app starts crashing or otherwise isn’t working properly for a significant number of your users. What should you do then?

items.title: Do you know what your mobile team is shipping right now?
items.summary: Every release requires dozens of questions to be asked and (eventually) answered. Those answers are apt to change throughout, and many of the individual questions may need to be asked multiple times by many stakeholders. This is untenable. Do you know what your mobile team is up to right now? Does your mobile team know what they’re up to right now? Does anyone?

items.title: AI will never build your app and your releases will never be fully automated
items.summary: Automation and AI are tools that humans wield, not magic spells that will take any idea we have and create it for us. We will always need to do the hard work of strategizing, planning, adapting, and building complex apps and systems in collaboration with other people.
